newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: World community gives mixed signals to Serb protesters.
newsitem.headline: World community gives mixed signals to Serb protesters.

text.p: Serbia's opposition pressed ahead with street protests after receiving both a rebuff and encouragement from the world community in action to drive President Slobodan Milosevic from power.
On Thursday -- 25th day of country-wide protests over alleged election fraud by his socialists -- Milosevic sent in riot police to stop a student march in Belgrade.

They blocked, without violence, a rally by more than 40,000 students intent on marching from central Belgrade to the exclusive Dedinje suburb where Milosevic and senior members of the government live.
Elsewhere on the streets of the capital 100,000 supporters of the Zajedno opposition coalition also rallied to force Milosevic's ouster.
Opposition parties suffered a set-back however when an international mediator urged them to ease their demands.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini met Milosevic and Zajedno leaders separately to try to end more than three weeks of upheaval since disputed elections on November 17.
Zajedno claimed the socialists cheated it of victory in the local elections in Belgrade and other towns and demanded Milosevic quit power and recognise their victory.
Dini said the opposition should rethink its objectives and told reporters:
"Reinstatement of the results seems to me to be something that is not on the cards as the basis for dialogue between the parties. They must find a formula around the impasse."
He said he found both sides "have dug themselves firmly into the positions from which they started."

But in a point for the opposition, head of Gremany's parliamentary delegation Christian Schwartz-Schilling told reporters he had warned Milosevic that it was useless to discuss economic assistance to the country until the election issue was solved.
"He said he could not understand why the international community was devoting such attention to these demonstrations," independent Belgrade radio B92 quoted him as saying.
Schwartz-Schilling said he suggested to Milosevic he call a commission of legal experts from the European Union and the United States to look into the matter.
"(Milosevic) said it might be a good idea because he wants to start solving the country's economic problems," he said.

The United States has considered re-imposing sanctions which would be a severe economic blow to Milosevic after the European Union's refusal of preferential trade privileges for Serbia because of the election conflict.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told CBS television that Milosevic would doom his hopes of ties with the West if he continued his "repressive, undemocratic stance".
The authorities have begun to take a tougher line since a young worker was arrested and beaten by police for carrying an effigy of Milosevic in prison garb at a march last week.
Belgrade actor Gojko Baletic who was arrested during Wednesday's demonstration suffered head and leg injuries before being released, his wife said.
The Serbian Drama Actors Guild reacted by cancelling all shows on Thursday in "a warning to all those using (police) batons that the theatre will not tolerate tyranny."
But Milosevic yielded ground by legalizing the popular B92 radio which gained world fame by its coverage of the protests and a two-day shutdown by the authorities as punishment.
Independent Belgrade B92 radio said it had signed a new 10-year contract with Radio and Television Serbia which allows it to broadcast via a state-owned transmitter.
